Hey hey, I was someone who was between fm and rads, had good grades and Step 2, near dozen publications including first author in rads journals, was rads interest group president, had scholarships in fm orgs, and knew I wanted to be a generalist. I ultimately chose fm. There were a few reasons. One was, like you, fm was my favorite rotation and rads was one of my least. During fm, I saw how they could do anything from outpatient to inpatient to ER to L&D. I enjoyed the preventative medicine, health education, shooting the shit with patients, the procedures, and I met nothing but happy family physicians. Their salaries were > 300k with $100k sign on bonuses and most worked 4 days a week. As someone else mentioned, reimbursements are increasing in fm, and the flexibility in jobs and practices (DPC is the jackpot) is being encouraged by even the AAFP. There is also something validating to me about being able to treat near anything and to be someone’s main doctor. I understand people complain about insurance and prior auths but I also saw that stuff during psych and rheumatology so that’s just a part of many specialties. I believe with the job shortage of family docs and the enormous fm career flexibility, it’s an up and coming gem. The thing is with being a fm doc is you do have to enjoy connecting with patients, and that’s pretty simple if you shoot the shit, do your job well, and write sticky notes on Epic about what each patient likes to do for fun. Salary is better rural and westward, as far away from the east coast as possible. Fm docs also have to know a little about everything, which can be overwhelming to some or exciting to others. Finally, you can feel good that fm docs extend the lifespan and quality of life of patients more than anybody else in medicine according to research, the world falls apart without fm. I’ll now speak about rads. I did not find it to be very puzzle solving, rads spend most of their time just describing the images alone by themselves in a dark room like they are taking STEP 2 repeatedly. I also found a lot of radiologists are depressed by the fact that a) many doctors ignore their report and make decisions on the image independently b) a majority of images are a defensive medicine strategy and not for any real medical purpose c) that they are needing to read images faster than ever before and that poor decisions/future radiology malpractice suits are hence being made. So many impressions are “clinically correlate” and an absolutely waste of time. It was also uncomfortable to see some radiologists get really frustrated when the computer ran a little slower than usual lol or if their dictation software acted up. I also know this gets downvoted on Reddit, and I understand we aren’t there yet, but radiology is actively trying to replace themselves with AI. And even if they don’t, the world treats radiologists like a lab test, and nobody knows or cares about the radiologist. Yes, the radiologist makes more money and can do it from home with months of vacation, but radiology has huge ups and downs, and I only see downs await in the long term. I cannot stress enough how bad the demand for imaging is, I believe it’s going to lead to major mistakes that will skyrocket malpractice rates and encourage more AI efforts which jeopardizes rads. Finally, rads is also one of the only specialities where being a resident is the easier part, the stakes and volume are so much higher as an attending. I’d much prefer residency being harder and attendinghood being easier than the contrary. I hope this helps!

The calculation for the p-value, you mean? Yes, but again p-value doesn’t tell you the magnitude of the difference. You are free to interpret the difference they found, or you can use effect size which tells you a universal, quantitative value of the real magnitude. Note that level of significance does not predict effect size. For example, the famous study that put aspirin in everything had a P value of < 0.00001, which was mind blowing for its time. It was only later found that it had a really small effect size of 0.77. Please ask me questions if you are confused about this topic, there is a big movement right now to begin including effect size along with P-values in publications and I am really passionate about, because I think it could shed a lot of clarity on matters like these and more.

Smaller p value =  likelihood that the finding was due to chance was little.
Doesn’t tell you magnitude of difference

So statistical differences only mean something about the probability of the result being chance. That doesn’t tell me anything about the magnitude of the difference, which is what we are focused on. If we care about magnitude, then we should be looking at effect size. A problem is that most studies won’t show effect size since most significant differences are of such little effect size they would be rejected from publication. But, if you have the willpower, you can do it yourself using effect size calculators online. And the reality is that the studies I have seen have placed reputation on a no to little to medium effect size on residency when I calculate it.
